Photograph: Newscom/Alamy US Capitol attack Natalie Harp reportedly posted 150 pro-Trump tweets on day of Capitol riot Devoted Trump aide flooded her now-disabled profile urging people to ‘never concede’ on 6 January 2021 Marina Dunbar Sun 23 Aug 2026 12.47 EDT Last modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 13.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Donald Trump aide Natalie Harp flooded a since-disabled social media account with pro-Trump posts on the day that the president’s supporters attacked the US Capitol in early 2021, years before she went to work for him and developed an extraordinary close relationship with him, a new report has revealed. CNN on Saturday reported that a deactivated account which Harp had on what is now known as X was packed with fiercely pro-Trump messages on the day of the January 6 Capitol attack in Washington DC, including posts repeating his lies that the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden toward the end of his first presidency, had been stolen from by fraudsters. “FIGHT FOR TRUMP!” Harp wrote 12 times in one of more than 150 posts that day alone. She followed that with a post declaring: “Today, DC is TRUMP COUNTRY!” Who is Natalie Harp? Trump’s closest and most devoted aide is in the spotlight Read more Among her other posts was the declaration “today we STOP THE STEAL!’”. And as Trump delivered a speech that day, Harp wrote: “We will never give up. We will never concede!” CNN’s reporting on those posts come as the US news media have put a spotlight on Harp, 35, and her near-constant presence at the side of Trump, 80, during his second presidency. The scrutiny has been fueled by intensely affectionate letters from Harp to Trump, including one in which she called him her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”; claims from her estranged brother that her relationship with the president is “ unhealthy ”; and a recent speech from Jon Ossoff, a Democratic senator from Georgia, who contended that one of the few things Trump wants to do is “travel with Natalie”. The social media account that CNN reported on, opened by Harp in 2016, also contained posts in which she compared Trump to a biblical figure, according to messages unearthed by the Daily Beast . “We all know the story of the Good Samaritan,” Harp wrote as she went on to recount her claim that an intervention by Trump had saved her life while she grappled with cancer. “But what you don’t know is I was that forgotten person on the side of the road – left to die of medical error and cancer. The Political Establishment passed me by. But @realDonaldTrump didn’t. Meet my Good Samaritan!” she wrote in the 2019 message. The X account now appears to be suspended. It remains unclear when it was taken down or whether Harp or the platform was responsible for removing the posts. Harp ’s official roles are special assistant to the president and executive assistant to the president – positions that come with an annual salary of $150,000. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion White House faces questions over security clearance for top Trump aide Natalie Harp Read more Inside Trump’s orbit, she has also earned the unofficial title of “ human printer ” – a reference to her role supplying the president with printed information. CNN’s report on Saturday also indicated that Harp’s embrace of Trump’s election-fraud narrative began well before the day of the Capitol insurrection. In the weeks leading up to the attack, she told followers: “We will never give up – for TRUTH is on our side. January 6th is coming!!” Her posts immediately following the election that ended Trump’s first presidency were similarly emphatic. “WE LOVE YOU! WE LOVE YOU! WE LOVE YOU!” Harp wrote days after the election results. Then, on 14 December 2020, as she denounced Biden’s victory, Harp posted: “THIS IS A COUP.” The resurfaced social media posts are not the only written materials now fueling scrutiny of Harp’s devotion to Trump. The Daily Beast published two intimate letters on Thursday written by the Trump aide in 2023. Beside calling him her “Guardian and Protector”, she wrote in one letter: “You are all that matters to me.” She also wrote: “I want to bring you joy, to feel like we can get through a day without ever having to talk ‘work.’” Explore more on these topics US Capitol attack Trump administration US politics Washington DC Donald Trump news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.freemalaysiatoday.com/catego.text: Ukrainian forces captured the North Korean soldiers early last year after thousands were deployed to support Russia's war. (EPA images pic) SEOUL: South Korean president Lee Jae Myung said Friday Seoul would take "further measures" if Ukraine refuses to publicly apologise over what he called its unilateral disclosure of North Korean POWs being sent to South Korea. Seoul has taken a hard stance on Ukraine disclosing the transfer of two soldiers captured fighting for Russia, warning that their families could be targeted by Pyongyang. The POWs were captured by Ukrainian forces early last year after being deployed alongside thousands of North Korean troops to support Russia's war against Ukraine, in exchange for economic and military assistance to Pyongyang. Hours after Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky disclosed last week the transfer in remarks at the United Nations, South Korea's Lee expressed his dismay, with Seoul claiming confidentiality was key to protecting the POWs' relatives. Seoul later demanded an official apology from Ukraine, saying that both sides had reached a "clear understanding" during consultations to keep the transfer confidential - citing concerns for the safety of the POWs' families in North Korea. "If Ukraine continues to refuse to acknowledge the facts and publicly apologise, we will take further measures," said the South Korean president on Friday, accusing Kyiv of making him out to be a "liar." "This is a matter concerning the dignity of the Republic of Korea and its people and cannot be overlooked," Lee posted on X. Analysts say that from South Korea's perspective, keeping the transfer of the POWs confidential may have partly been for Ukraine's sake, as making it public could have complicated Kyiv's own prisoner exchanges with Russia. In domestic South Korean politics, however, Seoul's approach "could prove problematic", Shin Yul, a political science professor at Myongji University, told AFP, given the current administration's dovish approach to the nuclear-armed North. "The government has acted swiftly in this case involving Ukraine, while exercising extreme caution over the North Korean landmine incident (that injured South Korean soldiers). That contrast could leave the public deeply dissatisfied." "Diplomatic misunderstanding" Lee referred on Friday to an interview with Ukraine's foreign minister Andrii Sybiha published by RBC-Ukraine and other Ukrainian outlets on Thursday. Sybiha said he would "not like to call it an incident", describing it instead as a "diplomatic misunderstanding". "South Korea is an important country for us. And I very much hope for momentum, continued cooperation, and concrete results that we are indeed achieving with them," he said. North Korea is known to retaliate against defectors and their families. Both POWs are identifiable as they had been photographed by South Korean media before their arrival to the South. Seoul's spy agency said that Zelensky may have disclosed the transfer of the North Korean soldiers to boost public support in South Korea for Seoul providing arms to Ukraine, a lawmaker said Wednesday. South Korea has in recent years emerged as a major arms exporter - particularly since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in early 2022 - including through a multibillion-dollar arms deal with Poland. But it has refrained from supplying Kyiv with lethal weapons, citing its longstanding policy of not arming countries engaged in active conflicts.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckj0.text: Figure caption, Carney: 'Canada must now serve' service members killed in fire By Paulin Kola Published 19 October 2026, 10:40 BST Updated 3 hours ago The fire that killed four members of the Canadian military and injured dozens of others on Saturday spread with alarming speed, accounts suggest. It broke out in a grassy training area at a base in the province of Alberta and spread rapidly due to strong winds. "The fire was 1km (0.6 miles) away when the wind shifted," said Maj-Gen Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division of the Canadian Armed Forces. "It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds." Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime". Officials have ruled out the possibility of "any terrorist activity". Speaking in the House of Commons on Monday, Carney said the fire was "driven by ferocious winds". "The fire jumped nearly a kilometer less than a minute to where the soldiers were gathered," he said, adding that the cause of the fire was not yet known. Carney said the injuries occurred "in the space of a few minutes". The blaze began at about 16:00 (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases. The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died. Of the 39 injured people receiving care in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told Canadian broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright. What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military base Published 3 hours ago Tributes are being paid to the servicemen who died. Patricia Farrell, the mother of Shaun Farrell, wrote on Facebook that it was "with heavy hearts that we share the news that our son, Shaun Farrell, has passed away to be with our Heavenly Father". Wong received a tribute from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, of which he was part. The regiment was "deeply saddened", it wrote in a Facebook post of its own. It sent "heartfelt condolences to [the group's] families, friends, and fellow soldiers". The mother of Goulding, Sonia Monk, said her late son was an exceptional athlete and a natural leader. "He was always the guy who kept everybody's spirits up," she told CBC. "He really was the light of my life." Canadian PM Carney said on Monday that Goulding was known as "a generous and deeply loyal friend". Lykkemark, Carney said, "was known for his gift for lightening a hard day, his quick wit - he dreamed of a career in law enforcement". "These were sons, brothers, partners, friends, young men with bright futures who chose to serve our country and who died in that cause," Carney said. Figure caption, Watch: Incident at Canadian military base 'unheard of', says local mayor In recounting Saturday's events, Rutland told reporters that members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range. He told reporters that officials knew about the fire on the base for several hours, but it was decided that training "could carry on for a certain amount of time". "I spoke to my commander last night, and he said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them," Rutland said. Rutland said it was not yet known what exactly caused the fire. Some witnesses had said they had heard explosions, fuelling speculation that oil and gas infrastructure may have been hit and sparked the fire. But Rutland said authorities "do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure". The Canadian Armed Forces has said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity". Forecasters had issued a wind warning on Saturday for large parts of Alberta, predicting wind gusts of up to 90km/h (66mph), Canadian broadcaster CBS said. According to Rutland, the investigation may take at least a month. Wainwright, about 130 miles east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day. Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Students and teachers in the hallway at an underground school in Kharkiv, Ukraine. Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The Guardian Ukraine Analysis ‘You are a humanitarian also, sir’: the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and die Andrew Roth in Kharkiv Steve Witkoff’s flattery of the Russian leader could be just the start of a mendacious stratagem from a US president who says Moscow ‘has been fine on Ukraine’ Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.57 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 14.54 EDT Share They say the first casualty of war is truth. For the Trump administration , the road to peace with Russia now encompasses some extraordinary lies. Steve Witkoff delivered one as he sat down with Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday, aiming to close the deal on Russia’s land grab in Ukraine with the White House’s strategy of maximum pressure on Kyiv and saccharine flattery of the Kremlin. “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” said Witkoff, a real-estate mogul who, thanks to being Trump’s friend, is now the US’s senior envoy and diplomat to end the largest European conflict since the second world war. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you.” In Putin’s 26 years in power, it is a rare moment when he has been granted that specific honour. Skim through Russia’s past wartime exploits – from the bombing campaigns in Chechnya and Georgia and Syria, to the thousands of Russian citizens jailed for dissent, to the violent deaths of prominent opposition journalists and politicians in barely disguised assassinations and poisonings – and it will be difficult to identify Putin’s credentials as a humanitarian. View image in fullscreen Vladimir Putin and Steve Witkoff meet in St Petersburg. Photograph: Kristina Solovyova/Reuters And that is before looking to Ukraine, where Russia chose to launch a full-scale invasion that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. The Guardian recently obtained a Russian strategy document showing the Kremlin’s potential to black out Ukrainian cities this winter, cutting off up to 90% of electricity to cities such as Kyiv and Odesa and Kharkiv – where millions of people live – to intentionally create a humanitarian catastrophe. And judging by the nightly barrages levelled at power plants for cities across Ukraine, the Kremlin has decided to move forward with that strategy until Kyiv surrenders. As Witkoff met Putin on Wednesday , schoolchildren in Kharkiv hastened down a reinforced stairway, sirens announcing the arrival of Shahed drones overhead. This is no ordinary bomb shelter; it is one of 10 underground schools Kharkiv has constructed because of Russia’s regular bombing of the city less than 20 miles from the border. Parents had welcomed the schools because they were safe, said teachers, and this was the one way that young people could have an uninterrupted school day during a war that could last years more – and reignite even if a shaky peace deal is reached. View image in fullscreen Students and parents arrive and depart from the entrance to an underground school in Kharkiv. Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The Guardian “We all believed in Trump. We all really had hopes for America and for Trump to stop this monster Putin,” said Olena Svytlychna, the head of the education department of the Novobavarskyi region in Kharkiv, sitting in the school’s cafe on Wednesday. “And now we have doubts, we don’t believe them. And we are very scared.” As Witkoff spoke, the families of six people killed in a drone strike in a park near Kharkiv this week were holding funerals. The youngest victim of the strike was a one-year-old girl, Anhelina, who was killed as she was sitting strapped into her stroller in a playground. Her mother, Inna Mariukhna, a local schoolteacher, was also killed in the strike. The final death toll was four adults and two children, Anhelina and an 11-year-old girl. View image in fullscreen A destroyed building in Kharkiv after an air attack on Tuesday. Photograph: Sergey Bobok/AFP/Getty Images Those lives have barely earned a mention from the White House as it pushes for Ukraine to capitulate as quickly as it can this week – and crucially before the 3 November midterm elections when voters will deliver a referendum on Trump’s leadership for the last two years. Shortly after the bombing, Trump told reporters on the White House lawn that Russia “has been fine on Ukraine”. After taking criticism for that remark, he mentioned the attacks in passing just to downplay the shelling of civilians: there were “some people in a town that got hit or whatever, but mostly young soldiers” died, he said from the Oval Office on Tuesday. For the White House, those words cost little. Witkoff’s goal was to bring home a US citizen, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan, who had been detained in Russia. But if Witkoff wants to buy a peace deal by 3 November through flattering Putin, then this will only be the White House’s opening salvo in its war on truth.
